segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where do the wars and where do the fights among you come from? Is it not from this—from your pleasures, which are at war in the members of your body?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You desire, and you do not have; you murder and envy, and you cannot obtain; you fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you think that the Scripture speaks to no purpose when it says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “He longs jealously for the spirit he made to dwell in us”?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he gives greater grace. That is why it says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “God opposes the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So submit to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned into mourning and your joy into gloom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. Whoever speaks against a brother or sister, or judges a brother or sister, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There is one lawgiver and judge—the one who is able to save and to destroy. But you—who are you to judge your neighbor?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Come now, you who say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Today or tomorrow we will travel to such-and-such a city and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: you who do not know what tomorrow holds—what your life will be! For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then disappears.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead you ought to say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So for anyone who knows the good they ought to do and does not do it, for that person it is sin.

notes.phrase: in the members of your body
notes.note: The Greek says simply “in your members,” meaning limbs or body parts. Most interpreters take this as the individual’s body, pictured as a battlefield of competing cravings. A minority take “members” as the members of the community, among whom the pleasures wage war.

notes.traditional: You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel.
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the clauses can be divided in more than one way. The translation follows the punctuation of the SBLGNT, which gives three parallel statements; many English versions instead divide so that murder is the result of frustrated desire and fighting the result of frustrated envy. Whether “murder” is literal or a deliberately shocking exaggeration is disputed.

The Greek word is feminine plural, “adulteresses.” It draws on the prophets’ picture of Israel as God’s unfaithful wife, so the charge is disloyalty to God, not sexual sin. Most modern versions paraphrase as “adulterous people”; later manuscripts expanded it to “adulterers and adulteresses,” which the King James Version follows.

No passage in the Hebrew Bible or its Greek translation matches the words that follow. They may summarize the scriptural theme of God’s jealousy for his people, quote a writing now lost, or—as some hold—the sentence may be a general statement about Scripture, with the actual quotation coming only in verse 6.

notes.phrase: He longs jealously for the spirit he made to dwell in us
notes.traditional: He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us
notes.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the letter. The Greek can also be read, “The spirit he made to dwell in us longs enviously,” describing the human tendency to envy; in favor of that reading, the word rendered “jealously” normally means envy, a vice not otherwise ascribed to God. The translation follows the majority of modern versions, which take God as the subject, in keeping with the image of unfaithfulness in verse 4. Some manuscripts read “the spirit that dwells in us.”

notes.phrase: “God opposes the proud, but to the humble he gives grace.”
notes.note: The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, with “God” in place of “the Lord.” The same text is quoted in 1 Peter 5:5. The introductory words can be read as “it says” (Scripture) or “he says” (God).

The Greek plural, traditionally “brothers” or “brethren,” was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women. James is speaking to the whole community, so the translation uses “brothers and sisters,” and “a brother or sister” for the singular later in the verse.

notes.phrase: what tomorrow holds—what your life will be
notes.traditional: you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life?
notes.note: The Greek is compressed, and the manuscripts differ slightly in wording. It can be read as one statement (“you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow”) or as a statement followed by a question (“What is your life?”). The sense is little affected.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters / a brother or sister
candidates.reason: The inclusive or masculine rendering of the plural address and the generic singular recurs in almost every letter and should be uniform.
Translators divide between “grace” and “favor,” and the word is central across the New Testament; here it sits inside a Proverbs quotation where “favor” is equally defensible.
The verb and its noun ζῆλος range from zeal to jealousy to envy, and the English needs a consistent policy by sense, especially alongside φθόνος.
Frequent in Paul and James with both positive and negative senses (“boast,” “glory,” “take pride”); a single policy would prevent drift.
Its negative sense, the human order opposed to God, recurs in John, Paul and James and should be rendered uniformly and distinguished from the neutral sense.
